extracted.intended_audience: biomedical investigators writing NIH grant applications (R01/resubmissions), especially early-career and mid-career PIs
extracted.subtask_short: nih grant writing for biomed PIs
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, experience-based guidance for writing competitive NIH-style biomedical grant applications (Specific Aims, Significance, Innovation, Approach, resubmissions). Emphasizes triage dynamics, reviewer psychology, preliminary data expectations, and resubmission tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for skim-reading reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers Are Tired and Skim — assume your assigned reviewer reads at midnight after dinner; the first paragraph of Significance must be self-contained; bold/underline matters more than you think — guide the eye; make every Aim title legible standalone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design text for rapid scanning: make opening sentences self-contained and informative, use typographic cues (bold/underline) to direct attention, and craft Aim titles so a reviewer can grasp intent without reading supporting text. Small visual and structural cues can determine whether a reviewer invests more time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific Aims page is critical for triage
rubrics_metrics.description: Triage Is the Real Game — half of submitted apps get triaged (not discussed); a triaged app gets ~12 minutes of attention from one reviewer; the Specific Aims page IS the application for triage purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the Specific Aims page as the application: it must present the hypothesis, aims, significance, and feasibility clearly and compellingly. If the Aims page fails, the whole application risk being triaged with minimal review time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid giving reviewers easy reasons to lowball
rubrics_metrics.description: Triage: avoid anything that gives the assigned reviewer an easy reason to lowball.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminate obvious weaknesses, ambiguous claims, or sloppy presentation on the front pages. Even minor avoidable problems can prompt a quick negative decision during triage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame innovation cautiously — favor feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Innovation Is a Trap — reviewers say they want innovation but reward feasibility; 'Highly innovative' + thin preliminary data = unscored; frame innovation as 'novel application of established methods' rather than 'no one has ever done this'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position novelty in a way that highlights feasibility and prior support. Tie innovative aspects to strong preliminary data or established methods to avoid signaling undue risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write to the three reviewer profiles
rubrics_metrics.description: The Three Reviewer Profiles — The Champion (advocates), The Hatchet (looks for killable flaws), The Indifferent (splits the difference). You must write for all three.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide ammunition for Champions (clear strengths and impact), leave no openings for Hatchets (tight methods, addressed weaknesses), and give Indifferents simple clear bullet points to follow. Balance enthusiasm with defensible rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary data hierarchy and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary Data Hierarchy — 1. Published in your lab >>> 2. Submitted/in review >>> 3. Unpublished from your lab >>> 4. From collaborators >>> 5. From the literature; anything below tier 3 is treated as suggestive at best; a figure caption that says '(unpublished)' must be supplemented elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maximize in-lab, preferably published, quantitative preliminary data (with effect sizes). If using unpublished or external data, explicitly contextualize credibility and supplement captions with methods or provenance to avoid being discounted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Junior PIs must over-document feasibility; use credible team members
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Old Boy' Reality — senior PIs get the benefit of the doubt; junior PIs must over-document feasibility; ESI status helps with paylines, not with substantive review; Co-Is with prior R01s buy you credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you are an early career investigator, provide extra feasibility evidence, methodological detail, and include experienced co-investigators to shore up credibility. Don't rely on status-based benefits in the review; demonstrate competence in the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resubmission strategy: address every critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Resubmission Strategy — address EVERY critique even if you disagree; use the Introduction page (one page allowed) to itemize changes; quote the reviewer directly when possible; even minor critiques must be acknowledged ('addressed by adding text on p.4'); never argue without conceding something.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On resubmission, respond point-by-point and visibly in the Introduction; show what changed and where. Be conciliatory—acknowledge reviewer concerns and show concrete steps taken, rather than arguing at length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach section must be rigorous and where reviewers find faults
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Approach' Section Is Where You Lose — Significance and Innovation get scored generously; Approach is where reviewers find faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize clarity and defensibility in Approach: include explicit methods, controls, and contingency plans. Anticipate methodological critiques and present clear, credible strategies to mitigate risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach must include key methodological elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Always include: rigor, sample sizes, statistical plan, alternative approaches, pitfalls, timeline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state sample size calculations/power analyses, statistical methods, blinding and randomization plans, alternative approaches if experiments fail, and a realistic timeline. Lack of these invites negative scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitfalls and alternatives must be realistic and reassuring
rubrics_metrics.description: Pitfalls and Alternatives Sections — a required ritual — write them or get dinged; show you've thought about what could go wrong; provide a backup that doesn't require the original to fail; don't list pitfalls so scary the reviewer worries the project will fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe plausible risks and practical backup plans that preserve project aims. Avoid describing catastrophic pitfalls without mitigation—this increases reviewer anxiety about project success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing voice: declarative, active, and jargon-minimized
rubrics_metrics.description: Write declaratively. 'We will determine X.' Never 'We hope to elucidate.' Active voice, first-person plural is fine in NIH grants; avoid jargon outside your subfield; define every acronym at first use, even obvious ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear, assertive language; prefer active constructions and concrete commitments. Minimize field-specific jargon and define acronyms to accommodate reviewers outside your immediate subfield.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit hypothesis and aims that test it
rubrics_metrics.description: What DrugMonkey Says Wins — Clear hypothesis explicitly stated; Aims that test the hypothesis (not 'characterize' or 'explore').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State a focused, testable hypothesis and write Aims that directly address its components. Avoid descriptive or exploratory framing that doesn't produce hypothesis-testing outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative preliminary data and power calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: What DrugMonkey Says Wins — Quantitative preliminary data with effect sizes. What Loses — No power calculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide measured effect sizes in preliminary data and include power/sample size calculations for planned experiments. Lack of quantitative support or power analysis is a common killer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a timeline figure
rubrics_metrics.description: What DrugMonkey Says Wins — A timeline figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a clear visual timeline for aims and milestones to demonstrate feasibility and project management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Team composition must visibly cover all required methods
rubrics_metrics.description: What DrugMonkey Says Wins — A team that visibly covers all the methods; Co-Is with prior R01s buy you credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the investigator team has demonstrable expertise for each major methodological component. Highlight specific roles and prior relevant experience to convince reviewers of feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor practices must be stated (SABV, blinding, randomization)
rubrics_metrics.description: What DrugMonkey Says Wins — Rigor language addressing sex as biological variable, blinding, randomization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly describe how rigor and reproducibility will be implemented (e.g., sex as a biological variable, blinding, randomization, data handling). Generic statements are weaker than concrete plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'fishing expedition' framing
rubrics_metrics.description: What Loses — 'Fishing expedition' framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame aims as hypothesis-driven tests with clear endpoints, rather than open-ended discovery without pre-specified criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid aim dependency (serially dependent aims)
rubrics_metrics.description: What Loses — Aim 1 must succeed for Aim 2/3 to work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure aims so that failure of one does not invalidate the entire project; provide parallelizable or standalone aims, or include contingency strategies to preserve downstream work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague 'we will use X to study Y' statements
rubrics_metrics.description: What Loses — Vague 'we will use X to study Y'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific about how methods will be applied, what outcomes will be measured, and how they address the hypothesis. Vague method statements undermine reviewer confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-including tangential citations/authors
rubrics_metrics.description: What Loses — Author lists too many tangentially relevant papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite and list collaborators selectively. Overloading references or author lists with tangential work dilutes focus and can signal lack of direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific Aims page must fit standard four-paragraph structure
rubrics_metrics.description: What Loses — Specific Aims page that doesn't fit standard four-paragraph structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the conventional four-paragraph Specific Aims structure (typically brief intro/significance, hypothesis/goals, aims, and impact/approach) so reviewers can find key information quickly and consistently.
